scenes.title: A brilliant colleague with no memory

s1b1.text: It's Tuesday morning. A message pops up: can we load this table from Statistics Netherlands, every day?

s1b2.text: One sentence. Ten years ago, that started a meeting. Today, you paste it into an AI agent, and code appears in minutes.

s1b3.text: Meet Tip. Tip is a small iceberg, and like every iceberg, most of Tip is under water.

s1b4.text: That turns out to be the whole story of building software with AI.

s2b1.text: Zoom out. Nine out of ten technology professionals now use AI at work.

s2b2.text: Almost three quarters of developers use coding assistants or agents every single day.

s2b3.text: But trust has not kept up. Only about one in six developers trusts AI with most everyday tasks. About half trust it when they can easily check the answer.

s2b4.text: And speed is harder to pin down than it feels. One careful study found experienced developers slower with early twenty twenty-five tools, and a little faster with later ones.

s2b5.text: Google's DORA research puts it simply: AI doesn't fix a team. It amplifies what's already there.

s3b1.text: Here's why. The code an agent writes is the tip of the iceberg. It's what everyone sees.

s3b2.text: What decides whether that code is any good sits below the waterline.

s3b3.text: Principles that guide every choice. Interfaces that people and agents share. Context the agent can read. And checks that catch mistakes.

s3b4.text: AI made the tip cheap. So the real work moved under the water.

s4b1.text: Take the data platform I build. It starts from five principles, and every change is checked against all five.

s4b2.text: API first means every button is an API call. So a script can do anything a person can.

s4b3.text: AI native means agents are users too. Every API call is also a tool an agent can use, through the Model Context Protocol, with the person's own identity and rights.

s4b4.text: In the pipelines extension, that's thirty tools. If a tool and its API call ever drift apart, a test fails.

s4b5.text: The protocol itself is open. By the end of twenty twenty-five it had moved to the Linux Foundation, with more than ten thousand public servers.

s5b1.text: The second thing to know about agents: an agent is like a brilliant new colleague who arrives every morning with no memory of yesterday.

s5b2.text: So what matters can't live in your head. It has to live in files.

s5b3.text: An agents file in every project tells the agent how to work there. More than sixty thousand open-source projects already have one.

s5b4.text: Skills are recipes for recurring jobs, like building a semantic model. And design records explain why a choice was made, before any code exists.

s5b5.text: DORA names this as one of the capabilities that make AI pay off: connect AI to your internal context.

s6b1.text: Back to Tuesday's question. Before writing code, the agent reads the code that's already there.

s6b2.text: It finds that pipeline runs have no internet, on purpose. So it proposes a separate extension for loading data, behind the same contract.

s6b3.text: It checks every licence, finds a library with copyleft terms, and swaps it for an open one.

s6b4.text: It compares newer tools. Then I decide: keep one as a candidate, and test it in a spike.

s6b5.text: Each step is checked against the five principles. And when code does come, the agent runs the full test suite, like the build server would, before it says done.

s6b6.text: The agent researches and proposes. The people decide.

s7b1.text: It's still Tuesday. The one-line question now has an answer: a design record, a principles check, and a plan for a spike.

s7b2.text: Not one line of production code yet. But when it comes, the agent can write it fast, because everything under the water is in place.

s7b3.text: AI makes the tip cheap. So build the part under the water.
